title: Vowel letters and Aramaic spelling

objectives.can: Read א, ה, ו and י as vowel letters where they are, and recognise the word-final א and ה of Aramaic.

explanation.summary: Four consonants, alef, he, vav and yod, are also used to write vowels. Aramaic leans on this more than the Hebrew you may know, and two of them, alef and he, end a great many Aramaic words. Knowing which of these letters is a vowel and which is a consonant is the first step in reading Aramaic words fluently.

sections.heading: Letters that stand for vowels
body: The vowel points of lesson A0.1.1 were added to the text by the Masoretes. Before them, scribes already used some consonant letters to hint at a vowel. These letters are called vowel letters (the older Latin name is matres lectionis, 'mothers of reading'). A vowel letter has no consonant sound of its own; it shows the vowel next to it. The points then say which vowel it is.

Vav and yod are the commonest. Vav can write the vowel ô or û: in the word for 'upon him' in Daniel 3:28, the vav carries a dot above it (a ḥolem) and writes ô; in the word for 'fire' in Daniel 3:6 the vav has a dot inside it (a shureq) and writes û. Yod can write î or ê: the plural ending of the word for 'kings' in Daniel 2:21 has a ḥiriq with a yod, and the word for 'house' in construct, found in Ezra 4:24, has a tsere with a yod. The fourth table of lesson A0.1.1 listed the points; the table below lists the letters that can write them.

The same letters are consonants in other places: a vav with its own vowel before it is the consonant w or v; a yod with a vowel under it or after a vowel can be the consonant y. The way to tell is to look at the pointing: a vowel letter has no vowel point of its own.

sections.heading: The final alef
body: A final alef after a qamets is the most characteristic ending in Aramaic. It marks the vowel ā at the end of a word, and in a noun it is usually the sign of the determined state, the Aramaic equivalent of the Hebrew definite article. The word for 'the king' in Daniel 2:4 is an example. Lesson A1.1.2 teaches the states. For now, learn to see the ending and to read it as a long ā.

The ending -ָא does not always show that a noun is determined. It also closes words that are not determined nouns: the negative word for 'not', the noun for 'counsel' in Daniel 2:14, and the adjective for 'great' in Daniel 2:6, where the alef follows a yod. It closes many verb forms as well: a final alef after tsere writes ē, for example in the verb in Daniel 3:6 that means 'will be cast'. So a final alef tells you only the vowel, not the grammar; the grammar comes from the word as a whole.

An alef can also be a consonant, with a vowel or a ḥatef of its own. In the word for 'God' the first letter carries a ḥatef segol and is a consonant, the catch in the throat. An alef with no point of its own after a vowel is a vowel letter or silent.

sections.heading: The final he, and alef and he for the same ending
body: A he at the end of a word, with no dot in it, is also a vowel letter. It writes ā or ē, as the alef does. It is the usual last letter of the pronoun 'this' and of verb forms like the participle in Daniel 2:5, where the he writes the vowel ē.

A he with a dot inside it (a mappiq) is a real consonant h. In Daniel 2:5 the word for 'its interpretation' ends in a he with a mappiq: the h is the pronoun 'his' or 'its', pronounced. The difference between a silent final he and a pronounced one is the dot, and no other mark.

The determined-state ending -ā is usually spelled with alef, but it is also spelled with he. The same noun can be written both ways: the word for 'the king' in Daniel 2:11 appears once with a he and once, a few words later, with an alef; the word for 'the house' appears with alef in Ezra 5:3 and with he in Ezra 6:15; the word for 'the people' appears with he in Ezra 7:13 and with alef in Ezra 7:16. These are not two words but two spellings of one ending. In both books alef is the commoner spelling; he is a minority spelling in both, and more frequent in Ezra than in Daniel.
When you read aloud, read both endings alike, as ā.

sections.heading: A first reading
body: Daniel 2:4 to 6 is the first Aramaic speech of the book. It has final alef in several nouns, a final he on a verb participle and a mappiq he, the vav of ô and û, and the yod of î. Read these verses aloud with the vowel letters in view, and for each word ask which letters are consonants and which are vowel letters.

misunderstandings: A final alef or he is not a consonant to be pronounced. A final alef after a qamets writes ā; so does a final he without a dot.
A final -ָא does not prove that a noun is in the determined state. It also ends words that are not determined nouns. Check the whole word.
A he with a dot (mappiq) is pronounced, but a he without a dot at the end of a word is not. The dot is the whole difference.
Alef and he spelling the same final ā is not a sign of two different words or two different grammatical forms. It is a spelling variant.

deeper.heading: Where the vowel letters came from
body: Scholars generally hold that the consonants alef, he, vav and yod came to be used as vowel letters first at the ends of words, in Aramaic and Hebrew, and then, over the centuries, inside them. The Masoretes' points were added later still, to fix the pronunciation of a text whose spelling already used these letters. As a result, the spelling of the Aramaic chapters preserves several stages. The variety between alef and he at the end of words, in the same chapter, is one sign of this.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Then spoke the Chaldeans to the king in Aramaic: 'O king, live for ever! tell thy servants the dream, and we will declare the interpretation.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Three nouns of one verse each ending in a qamets and an alef: 'the king', 'the dream' and 'the interpretation' (the last with a vav 'and' in front). The final alef writes ā, and in each of them it is the sign of the determined state. The alef is not pronounced as a separate consonant.

examples.analysis: The word for 'king' appears twice in this verse, with the same meaning: once with a final he and once, in the eleventh word, with a final alef. Both write the same final ā. This is a real instance of the two spellings.

examples.analysis: The first of these has a yod after a ḥiriq near the end, a vowel letter that writes î. In the second the vav, with a dot above it, writes ô, then comes a consonant he, then a final yod that writes î: this is the ending 'his'. The third is also a vav of ô, followed by the same ending.

reading.why: The first Aramaic speech of Daniel has final alef in several nouns, the he of a verb participle, a he with a mappiq, and the vowel letters vav and yod. Read the three verses aloud and name each vowel letter as you meet it.
